(i) FOMC participants were aware of the acceleration of labor productivity growth as early as the first half of 1996; (ii) the acceleration of labor and total factor productivity was the most important factor in explaining the rapid output growth of the late 1990s, with the acceleration in labor productivity growth being more important than the acceleration in capital deepening; (iii) FOMC members were aware that the acceleration of productivity was not due to a cyclical rebound, but to
the FOMC's assessment of the productivity growth slowdown was correct, and that it was based on an accurate reading of the record.

(1) the productivity growth slowdown of the 1970s and early 1980s was not a surprise, (2) FOMC participants had a clear sense of the productivity acceleration in the mid-1990s, and (3) FOMC policymakers had a clear sense that the productivity growth of the 1990-2001 period was not sustainable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how policymakers use the available information to assess the underlying state of the economy.
the process of information acquisition and learning by the Federal Reserve.
the process by which FOMC members learned about the acceleration of productivity growth and the implications of this learning for the conduct of monetary policy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
productivity growth was indeed higher in the 1995-2000 period, but it was not clear to the participants in the FOMC meetings until the second half of 1999.
FOMC participants were not able to identify the 1996-2004 productivity acceleration until after the fact.
the FOMC was not able to identify the productivity growth acceleration in the early years of the 1990 to 2000 expansion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FOMC's learning process is consistent with the standard economic model of learning.
the FOMC was aware of a productivity acceleration in the late 1990s but did not fully appreciate its magnitude until the early 2000s.

the Fed was slow to identify the productivity acceleration, and that this slowness was due to the difficulty of distinguishing between a cyclical recovery from a recession and a structural shift in the underlying trend of productivity growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FOMC did not ignore the firm-level evidence; instead, the FOMC was skeptical of it, as it was based on anecdotal evidence rather than hard data.
